sentences.text: Find the four chambers in the heart.
The right atrium and left atrium receive returning blood.
The right ventricle and left ventricle eject blood.
The septum separates the right and left sides.
Now trace the two connected routes.
Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle, and travels to the lungs.
Blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle, and leaves for the body.
Both sides pump during the same heartbeat, but toward different destinations.
The right side supplies the pulmonary circuit.
The left side supplies the systemic circuit.
Pause here and point to each chamber.
Use the patient's right and left, even when the front view reverses them on your screen.
Start the blood-flow journey at the right atrium.
The superior vena cava returns blood from much of the upper body.
The inferior vena cava returns blood from much of the lower body.
The coronary sinus returns much of the blood that has supplied the heart muscle itself.
This returning blood contains less oxygen than blood leaving the lungs, but it is not completely without oxygen.
Follow blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
Tricuspid means three cusps.
This is an atrioventricular valve, because it lies between an atrium and a ventricle.
When ventricular pressure rises, the valve closes and limits backward flow into the atrium.
Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles help keep the valve cusps from prolapsing backward during contraction; they do not pull the valve open.
The right ventricle ejects blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which branches toward the two lungs.
The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve.
Its pocket-like cusps limit backward flow into the ventricle after ejection.
Arteries are named for carrying blood away from the heart, not for carrying oxygen-rich blood.
The pulmonary arteries are the important example: they carry relatively oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs.
In the pulmonary capillaries, blood comes close to air inside the alveoli without normally mixing with that air.
Oxygen moves into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves toward the alveolar air.
The pulmonary veins then return relatively oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium.
Usually four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium.
A vein carries blood toward the heart, so pulmonary veins remain veins even though their blood is oxygen-rich.
Blood passes from the left atrium through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
The mitral valve is also called the bicuspid valve because it normally has two cusps.
Notice the thicker muscular wall of the left ventricle.
It must generate the pressure needed for systemic circulation.
Compare wall thickness, not a claim that the left ventricular chamber is always larger.
In a steady state, both ventricles pump approximately the same volume per minute.
The left ventricle ejects blood through the aortic valve into the aorta.
From there, arteries branch into smaller arteries and arterioles.
Capillary networks bring blood close to tissue cells.
After exchange, blood enters venules and veins, eventually returning to the right atrium.
The aortic valve is the second semilunar valve.
Like the other valves, it opens and closes in response to pressure differences across it.
The pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series.
Pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left atrium.
Systemic circulation runs from the left ventricle through the body to the right atrium.
The heart's own coronary circulation is part of the systemic circuit.
Blood-flow arrows should always follow this route.
Red and blue are teaching colors for relative oxygen content; human blood is never actually blue.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it toward the heart.
Arterioles regulate resistance and distribute flow.
Capillaries are thin exchange vessels.
Larger vessels have an inner tunica intima, a middle tunica media, and an outer tunica externa.
The lumen is the open space inside.
Vasoconstriction narrows the lumen; vasodilation widens it.
Many veins have valves that help limit backward flow, especially in the limbs.
Blood contains plasma and formed elements.
Plasma is the liquid transport medium.
Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which carries most blood oxygen.
White blood cells participate in immune defense.
Platelets help form clots.
Carbon dioxide travels in several forms, especially as bicarbonate in plasma.
Tissue perfusion means blood flowing through tissues; adequate oxygen delivery also depends on the amount of hemoglobin, its oxygen saturation, and the flow reaching those tissues.
The heart muscle needs its own blood supply.
Coronary arteries branch from the aorta.
Major vessels include the right coronary artery and the left coronary artery, which gives rise to the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries.
Cardiac veins return much of this blood through the coronary sinus.
Left ventricular coronary flow is greatest during diastole, largely because contraction compresses vessels in the ventricular wall.
Valve closure is not a switch that turns coronary flow on.
Now trace a complete circuit yourself.
Begin at the right atrium.
Name each valve and chamber, visit the lungs, return to the left side, and leave through the aorta.
Then explain two exceptions to the shortcut that arteries contain oxygen-rich blood and veins contain oxygen-poor blood.
Use the actual definitions: away from the heart for arteries, toward the heart for veins.
